rv.q: Absolute Hell is bold and ambitious, fascinating and provocative.
It's sometimes deceptively difficult viewing, but it's well worth meeting the challenge.
Ackland’s myopic drunkards simply embody the raffish bohemia of postwar Soho.
It’s a lot of fun to watch: we love seeing other people behaving terribly, after all, and set in an anything-goes Soho, this lot are deliciously bad.
Yet this three-hour evening does have its moments, if only as a reminder of grimmer days.
Depending on your view, then, this is a glass half-empty or half-full revival but not, perhaps surprisingly, an absolute must.
What should be swift and cutting is here simply slow.
This play is a slow burn that rarely flickers into life.
The Beeb should snap up this tragicomic fiesta and turn it into a series.
Director Joe Hill-Gibbins' production is a deliberately slow-burn, but the three hours it takes are captivatingly detailed.

With standout performances from Kate Fleetwood, Charles Edwards and Jonathan Slinger, along with fine cameos from a whole team of stars, this revival is highly enjoyable but also thought-provoking and well worth a visit.
Absolute Hell is fun, but this time the show is better than the writing.

It is a world perfectly depicted in Lizzie Clachan’s crumbling set, yet the production fails to get to the heart of Ackland’s script, relying too much on gimmicks to distract the audience from the text.
After a while, it is difficult to feel much sympathy.
On this showing, it is so far from a masterpiece that it is best left as a brave curiosity in the drawer marked history.
Ackland more than earns the title with this picture of a society about to face change, a sharp critique that is also very funny.
Their good work goes a long way to saving what is hyped as a classic, but is actually not such a very good play.
Joe Hill-Gibbins' production is over-stylised and detached with many of the ensemble too often hidden away in rooms of Lizzie Clachan's huge set.

cn.t: This sprawling 1952 Soho drama about a boozy postwar drinking club divides critics: some praise its ambitious ensemble and bold social portrait, while others find it overlong and unable to sustain its symbolic weight across three hours.
